title: Unique Paths II
prompt: A robot sits at the top-left corner of an `m x n` grid, given as `obstacle_grid`, where `1` marks a cell containing an obstacle and `0` marks a free cell. The robot can only move down or right at any point, and cannot step onto a cell containing an obstacle. Return the number of distinct paths from the top-left to the bottom-right corner. If either the start or end cell contains an obstacle, there are 0 valid paths.

examples.explanation: The obstacle in the middle forces exactly two distinct paths around it.
When the starting cell itself is an obstacle, the robot can never begin moving, so there are 0 valid paths regardless of the rest of the grid.

hints: This builds directly on the obstacle-free path-counting problem — the recurrence is almost the same, you just need to handle blocked cells.
Define dp[r][c] as the number of paths to reach (r, c). If a cell has an obstacle, dp[r][c] = 0 regardless of anything else, since the robot can never occupy it.
For a free cell, dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1], but treat out-of-bounds neighbors as contributing 0 rather than assuming the whole first row/column is 1 like in the obstacle-free version.

solution.approach: Same core recurrence as counting unique paths, but any cell containing an obstacle is forced to 0 reachable paths since the robot can never stand there. Build dp[r][c] left-to-right, top-to-bottom: if obstacle_grid[r][c] is 1, dp[r][c] = 0. Otherwise dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1], treating any neighbor that's out of bounds as 0. Special-case the very first cell: dp[0][0] = 1 only if it isn't itself an obstacle. The answer is dp[m-1][n-1].
